newsitem.title: JORDAN: Iraq's U.N. deal boosts shares in neighbour Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's U.N. deal boosts shares in neighbour Jordan.

text.p: Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the U.N. breathed new life into Jordan's flagging stock market on Wednesday, boosting industrial and pharmaceutical shares which hope to gain most from renewed oil sales by their sanction-hit neighbour.

Share prices rose 1.22 percent in busy trade, breaking out of the trough they sank into two months ago when fighting in the West Bank and northern Iraq depressed hopes that two of Jordan's natural export markets would open up in the near future.

"The Iraqi news is probably 80 percent of the reason for this recovery," said broker Nasser al-Amad, adding that end-of-year book keeping was also playing a role as major investors tried to prop up portfolios before their auditing.

Iraq said on Monday it had agreed to all U.N. conditions that had held up implementation of the oil-for-food deal, agreed in May but delayed by the August fighting in the Kurdish north Iraq, and predicted oil would start flowing next month.
The Amman Financial Market 60-share index rose 1.81 points to end the trading week on 150.05 points, its highest level for ten weeks, in healthy trade worth 1.09 million dinars ($1.54 million).
"We said the market was bottoming out and any good news will give it in an upward trend," said Amad, general manager of United Financial Investments.

Industrial companies Universal Modern Industries and National Industries both rose by the maximum five percent limit in one trading session to close at 1.60 dinars and 0.60 dinars in trade worth over 30,000 dinars each.
Arab Pharmaceutical Manufacturers also rose strongly by 0.16 dinars to 3.28 in trade worth 79,000 dinars.
Pharmaceutical firms expect to benefit from Iraqi purchases of urgently needed medicines.

Industrial firms, some of which sell goods like detergents not covered by the tough U.N. sanctions slapped on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, also see the deal as a firm step towards the full lifting of the embargo.

Jordanians who fled Kuwait after the invasion are also expected to benefit from the deal, which allows Iraq to export $2 billion of oil every six months and allocates 30 percent of those revenues to a U.N. Gulf War reparations fund.
"I think down the road we will see a better prices and turnover on the market," Amad said. "We will see a turn in economic cycle -- more Iraqi trade and compensation to the Jordanian expatriates."
Gaining shares outnumbered losers by 37 to six, with another five trading but closing unchanged.

Arab Bank, the biggest stock on the market in terms of capitalisation, rose four dinars to a one-year high of 252.50 dinars in busy turnover of 332,000 dinars, boosted by the general positive sentiment on the exchange.
Investors expect the bank to announce a share split to transfer capital from reserves within weeks.
The private Pearl Consulting index of Amman's 45 best-traded shares rose 1.10 percent to 80.37, still 15.85 percent down on last year.
